about_score_intro: Each of the six stats runs from 0 to 100. The overall rating is their weighted average, using the shares below.
about_stat_imp: Stars and forks on your repos
about_stat_rep: PRs merged into other people's repos, and code reviews
about_stat_exp: How many years you've been building
about_story_1: We turn your GitHub contributions, stars and PRs into a collectible card game: get your card, duel a friend, see where you land on the leaderboard. Scores only measure visible work; the real fun is in the comparing.
about_score_note: The first points come quickly and the top gets harder: full marks take extreme values (for example {followers} followers). Most active developers get silver or gold; 90+ is for the very best.
about_privacy_body: All data comes from GitHub's public API. Private repos are never read, and no email or other contact details are stored. Anonymous, cookie-free visit statistics help improve the site.
about_lead: Turns a public GitHub profile into a collectible card. Scores come from open formulas, not AI.
about_faq_low_q: Why is my rating lower than I expected?
about_faq_low_a: Gitscout can only see your public work on GitHub. Work in private repos, closed company projects or on other platforms like GitLab isn't counted. Ratings also grow logarithmically: the first points come easily, but each point near the top takes far more contributions.
about_faq_refresh_a: Cards refresh on their own every {days} days. Activity looks at the last year, so new contributions push your rating up while older ones gradually drop out, which means your rating can go up and down. If a mistake or unfairness turns up in the formula, it gets fixed and everyone's rating is recalculated.
about_faq_bots_q: Do automated commits inflate my rating?
about_faq_bots_a: No. At most {daily} contributions count per day; anything beyond that is ignored. If more than {repo} commits a year go into a single repo, they're treated as automation and deducted from your activity.
about_faq_org_q: How is my work in organization repos counted?
about_faq_org_a: Stars and forks on your own repos count fully toward Impact. On an organization repo, you get a share of its stars equal to your share of its commits. That share is the larger of your share over the last year and over the repo's whole history, so both the person who started a project and the one running it today get their due. Commits by AI agents such as Claude, Copilot and Codex, and by bots, are left out, so work you did with an agent counts as yours. If your commits were made with an email that isn't linked to your GitHub account, GitHub doesn't credit them to you and Gitscout can't see them either. PRs to organizations where your commit share is {share} or more count at {weight} weight in Reputation.
about_faq_role_q: How are my role and badges decided?
about_faq_role_a: Your role comes from the languages in your repos, and the area with the biggest share becomes your role. If both Frontend and Backend are at {share} or more, you're Full Stack. Badges highlight achievements like long contribution streaks or lots of code reviews; they don't affect your rating.
about_faq_flag_q: Why does my card show the wrong country's flag?
about_faq_flag_a: Your country is detected automatically from the location field on your GitHub profile. For example, a Turkish developer living in the Netherlands who wrote Amsterdam as their location gets a Dutch flag. To fix it, log in with GitHub and pick your country yourself on the Settings page; the country you choose shows on your card, your profile and the leaderboard.
about_privacy_removal: Anyone can add any username. If you'd rather not be on the leaderboard, open an issue and your card will be removed.

readme_badge_hint: Shows your rating and card tier on your profile README, and updates on its own whenever your card refreshes.
about_badge_body: You can add a Gitscout badge to your GitHub profile README. It comes in three sizes: a mini badge with your overall rating and card type, a medium card that adds your six stats, and your full player card. Whichever you pick updates itself as your card refreshes, and clicking it opens your Gitscout card. To get it, open your card's page and choose README badge from the Share menu; you don't need to log in. If you're logged in, the same section is also on the Settings page. Pick a size there, then copy the ready code and paste it yourself, or hand the ready prompt to an AI agent and let it do the work.
